Right-click the session group on the Data Properties and Settings panel and then choose Export > As ORSObject in the pop-up menu.
Click the Export Object button on the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Choose a location and file name in the Export to File dialog and then save the file.
How to Import a Session Group
Do one of the following:
Click the Import Object button on the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Choose File > Import Object(s) on the menu bar.
Navigate to, choose, and then open the required Dragonfly Object file in the Import Object(s) dialog.
The Select Objects dialog appears.
Note You can also import a session group from a saved session. In this case, select the Session file (*.ORSSession extension) with the required group and then select the session group that you want to import in the Select Objects dialog.
Select the object(s) that want to import and then click OK.

documents.title: Segmentation Wizard
documents.text:
Segmentation Wizard
Dragonfly’s Segmentation Wizard provides an easy-to-use, guided workflow for training deep learning and machine learning (classical) models for semantic image segmentation. With the Segmentation Wizard, you simply paint the different features of interest within a limited subset of your image data and then train models according to a predefined set of rules. The most promising model can then be fine-tuned and published for repeated segmentation tasks.
In This Section
Videos About the Segmentation Wizard
Segmentation Wizard Interface
Model Generation Strategies
Generating New Models
Working with Multiple Datasets
Working with Multi-Modality Models
Training Parameters for Deep Models
Training Models with the Segmentation Wizard
Segmentation Wizard Session Groups

documents.path: Artificial Intelligence/Segmentation Wizard/Training Models with the Segmentation Wizard.htm
documents.title: Training Models with the Segmentation Wizard
documents.text:
Training Models with the Segmentation Wizard
With the Segmentation Wizard, you simply paint the different features of interest within a limited subset of your image data and then train models to identify objects according to a predefined set of rules. The most promising model can then be fine-tuned and published for repeated segmentation tasks. The main tasks for training semantic segmentation models with the Segmentation Wizard are labeling classes in frames, choosing a model generation strategy, and then training the models within the selected strategy.
Labeling Frames for Training
You can use any of the segmentation tools available on the ROI Painter and ROI Tools panels to label the voxels within a frame for training a model (see Labeling Multi-ROIs). The classes and labels defined for training are available in the Classes and labels box, as shown below.
Classes and labels box
You should note that you can train deep models with sparse labeling as of version 2024.1. In previous versions, deep models could only be trained with dense labeling.
Sparse labeling… In this case, only a limited number of voxels are labeled. However, after the first training cycle is completed or stopped, you can then populate frames with the best prediction, edit the results, and then continue training. An example of sparse labeling is provided below.
Sparsely labeled frame
Dense labeling… In this case, all voxels within a frame are labeled. An example of a fully segmented frame is provided below.
Densely labeled frame
Enabling Visual Feedback and Checkpoint Caches
To help monitor and evaluate the progress of training deep models, you can designate a frame for visual feedback. With the Visual Feedback option selected, the model’s inference will be displayed in the Training dialog in real time as each epoch is completed, as shown on the right of the screen capture below. In addition, you can create a checkpoint cache so that you can save a copy of the model at a selected checkpoint (see Saving and Loading Model Checkpoints). Saved checkpoints are marked in bold on the plotted graph, as shown below.
Training dialog
How to Enable Visual Feedback
Add a frame to an area that does not include any labels.
Double-click inside the corresponding User for box and then choose Monitoring in the drop-down menu, as shown below.
Training Models
You can start training models for semantic segmentation in the Segmentation Wizard after you have labeling at least one frame.
You should note that the initial set of training parameters should work well in most cases. Refer to Training Parameters for Deep Models for information about editing the training parameters of deep models. You should also note that the training parameters and weights are saved with each model and can be reused for future training.
Refer to the topic Working with Multi-Modality Models if you plan to work with multi-modality images. You should also refer to the topic Working with Multiple Datasets if you plan to work with multiple datasets.
How to Train a Model
Do one of the following:
On the Data Properties and Settings panel, right-click the image data that you want to train the models with and then choose Segmentation Wizard in the pop-up menu.
Choose Artificial Intelligence > Segmentation Wizard on the menu bar.
In this case, you can choose to create a new Segmentation Wizard session or to open a loaded Segmentation Wizard session (see Loading Session Groups).
The Model Selection dialog, shown below, appears.
Note Refer to the topics Working with Multiple Datasets and Working with Multi-Modality Models if you need to load multiple images.
Do the following in the Model Selection dialog, as required.
Select a previously trained model in the Model drop-down list.
Click the Open Remote Library button and then download a ready-to-use model in the Remote Library of Ready-to-Use Segmentation Models dialog. See Ready-to-Use Deep Models for additional information about working with ready-to-use models.
Do one of the following:
Click the Start with Model button if you want to start the session with the selected previously trained model. In this case, the trained model will appear on the Models tab.
Click the Start without Model button if you want to start the session without a trained model. In this case, you generate new models to start with or you can import a trained model.
The Segmentation Wizard appears onscreen (see Segmentation Wizard Interface).
Adjust the view so that the area you plan to label first is maximized in the view (see Using the Manipulate Tools).
Note Refer to the topic Window Leveling for information about adjusting the brightness and contrast.
Click the Add button in the Frames box.
A new frame is added to the main view in the workspace and two classes appear in the Classes and labels box. You can adjust the size and position of the frame, if required.
Note If have already prepared a multi-ROI with the required labeling, you can fill the frame by right-clicking and then choosing Fill Frames from Multi-ROI. In this case, you then need to select the multi-ROI in the Choose a Multi-ROI dialog, shown below.
Note Only labeled multi-ROIs that have the same geometry as the input dataset will be available in the drop-down menu.
Do the following, as required:
Add additional classes.
To add a class or classes, click Add in the Classes and labels box and then choose Add Class or Add Multiple Classes. If you are adding multiple classes, choose the number of classes to add in the Add Classes dialog.
Rename the classes and change the assigned colors, recommended.
Label the classes with the ROI Painter tools, as required (see Labeling Frames for Training).
You can deploy two different labeling strategies to train new models — sparse labeling and fully segmented patches. In many cases, you should be able to achieve comparable results with sparse labeling to those obtained by training with densely labeled ground truths, which can be much more laborious to obtain.
Note If you are training with multiple modalities, you can switch the image data shown in the frame by selecting another item in the Image modalities box, as well as with keyboard shortcuts Show Next Image Modality and Show Previous Image Modality (see Working with Multi-Modality Models).
Note If you are training with multiple datasets, you can switch the image data shown in a frame by selecting another dataset in the Data sets box, shown below (see Working with Multiple Datasets).
Add additional frames and continue labeling classes, as required.
Add a frame for visual feedback, if you plan to generate deep models (see Enabling Visual Feedback and Checkpoint Caches).
Designate a usage for each frame, as required (see Frames and Frame Usage).
Click Train.
The Model Generation Strategy dialog appears if you started the session without a trained model (see Model Generation Strategies).
Select a strategy, as required.
If required, you can deselect any of the models in the selected strategy. Deselected models will not be generated when you click Continue.
You should note that greyed out models cannot be generated currently. This could be due to sparse labeling, inadequate labeling, or another issue.
Note If required, you can edit the parameters of deep models and the feature presets of machine learning (classical) models for the current Segmentation Wizard session (see Deep Learning Model Types and Machine Learning (Classical) Model Types).
Click Continue.
The selected models are generated one-by-one and then the dataset(s) is validated and automatically split into training, validation, and test sets. For deep models, you can monitor the progress of training in the Training Model dialog, as shown below.
During deep model training, the quantities 'loss' and 'val_loss' should decrease. You should continue to train until 'val_loss' stops decreasing. You can also select other metrics, such as 'F1Score' to monitor training progress.
Note You can also click the List tab and then view the training metric values for each epoch.
When training is completed or stopped, up to the best three results appear at the bottom of the workspace.
Evaluate the model predictions in the Prediction views, recommended.
Each model prediction view includes the name of the corresponding model and includes the following controls:
Clicking the Up arrow fills the current frame with the selected model prediction.
The Default Model checkbox lets you select the model that will be used to automatically fill frames whenever the 'Automatically fill new frames with best prediction' option is selected on the Settings tab (see Settings Tab).
Note The number of predictions shown is selectable on the Models tab (see Models Tab).
If the results are not satisfactory, you should consider doing one or more of the following and then retraining the model(s):
Add an additional frame or frames to provide more training data.
Note You can fill additional frames from a multi-ROI or from a prediction. These options are available in the pop-up menu for frames.
Add a different model (see Generating New Models).
Adjust the parameters of a model (see Training Parameters for Deep Models).
When the model or models are trained satisfactorily, click the Exit button.
You can then select the model or models that you want to publish in the Publish Models dialog, shown below.
Note You need to 'publish' a model to make it available to other features of Dragonfly, such as Segment with AI (see Segment with AI) and the Deep Learning tool (see Deep Learning Tool).
The Segmentation Wizard session is saved and a new session group appears on the Data Properties and Settings panel (see Segmentation Wizard Session Groups).

documents.path: Artificial Intelligence/Segmentation Wizard/Training Parameters for Deep Models.htm
documents.title: Training Parameters for Deep Models
documents.text:
Training Parameters for Deep Models
The default training parameters for deep models should work well in most cases. However, you can edit the training parameters if your results are not satisfactory.
Right-click the deep model you need to edit on the Models tab and then choose Update Training Parameters in the pop-up menu to open the Training Parameters dialog, shown below.
Training Parameters dialog
The Training Parameters dialog includes three tabs — Settings, Advanced Settings, and Data Augmentation — as well as a number of options for applying and saving changes, which are described below.
Save as Defaults… Saves the current settings as the default values, which will be applied to new models.
Load Defaults… Restores the model settings to the last saved default values.
Reset Defaults… Resets all model settings to their original values.
Apply to… The Apply to options include the following:
Current model only. If selected, all changes will be applied to the selected deep model only.
All current deep models. If selected, all changes will be applied to all deep models in the current Segmentation Wizard session.
Settings
The following basic settings, which include patch and batch sizes, stride ratio, and epochs number, as well as loss function and optimization algorithm, are available on the Settings tab.
Settings tab
Description
Patch size
During training, training data is split into smaller 2D data patches, which is defined by the 'Input (Patch) Size' parameter.
For example, if you choose a Patch size of 64, the Deep Learning Tool will cut the dataset into sub-sections of 64x64 pixels. These subsections will then be used as the training dataset. By subdividing images, each pass or 'epoch' should be faster and use less memory.
Batch size
Patches are randomly processed in batches and the 'Batch size' parameter determines the number of patches in a batch.
Auto-set… Sets an optimized batch size based on available memory, the selected model, and patch size. This initial estimate may change during training, but is capped at 64. You should note you will need to choose 'Custom' to set any batch size larger than 64.
Custom… Lets you manually select a batch size. You should monitor the 'Estimated memory ratio' whenever you set this parameter yourself.
Estimated memory ratio… Displays the estimated memory ratio, which is calculated as the ratio of the estimated memory needed to train the model at the current settings over the available GPU memory. This ratio is shown whenever 'Custom' is selected as the 'Batch size' setting. You should note that the memory needed to train a deep model is dependent on the depth of the model, as well as the selected patch and batch sizes.
Green … The estimated memory requirement is within your system's capabilities, typically less than 0.90.
Yellow … The estimated memory requirement is approaching your system's capabilities. Ratios between 0.90 and 1.00 may or may not result in successful training. You can adjust the batch and/or patch size to reduce the estimated memory requirement.
Red … The estimated memory requirement exceeds your system's capabilities. You should consider adjusting the model training parameters, such as the batch and/or patch size, or selecting a shallower model. Training often fails when ratios are greater than 1.0.
Stride ratio
Specifies the overlap between adjacent patches.
At a value of '1.0', there will be no overlap between patches and they will be extracted sequentially one after another. At a value of '0.25', there will be a 25% overlap. You should note that any value greater than '1.0' will result in gaps between data patches.
Note The stride ratio applies only during training. At inference time, patch tiling and stitching are managed automatically by Dragonfly (see How Images are Tiled During Inference).
Epochs number
A single pass over all the data patches is called an 'epoch', and the number of epochs is controlled by the 'Epochs number' parameter.
Loss function
Loss functions, which are selectable in the drop-down menu, measure the error between the neural network's prediction and reality. The error is then used to update the model parameters.
Note Refer to Loss Functions for Semantic Segmentation Models for additional information about the available loss functions.
Optimization algorithm
Optimization algorithms are used to update the parameters of the model so that prediction errors are minimized. Optimization is a procedure in which the gradient — the partial derivative of the loss function with respect to the network's parameters — is first computed and then the model weights are modified by a given step size in the direction opposite of the gradient until a local minimum is achieved.
The Segmentation Wizard provides several optimization algorithms — ASGD, Adadelta, Adafactor, Adagrad, Adam, and others — which work well on different kinds of problems. Refer to Optimization Algorithms for additional information about the available optimization algorithms and editable settings.
Advanced Settings
The following advanced settings, which let you set learning rate patience and cooldown as a fraction of the available training data available, as well as set early stopping patience, are available on the Advanced Settings tab.
A. Learning rate scheduler and editable parameters B. Early stopping callback and editable parameters
Learning Rate Scheduler
The learning rate scheduler dynamically adjusts the learning rate of an optimizer (see Optimization Algorithms) during the training process to help accelerate convergence. Instead of using a fixed learning rate throughout training, which can lead to suboptimal convergence or slow training, schedulers modify the learning rate based on predefined rules or the model's performance. Refer to Learning Rate Scheduler for information about setting learning rate schedulers.
You should note the following whenever you edit the 'Patience' and 'Cooldown' settings for the 'Reduce Learning Rate On Plateau' scheduler:
Training voxel count corresponds to the number of labeled voxels in all Mixed/Training frames and takes into account the data augmentation factor and stride ratio.
With the 'As a fixed value' option checked, the computation section will be disabled and the behavior will be 'normal'.
With the 'Using the following computation' option checked, the 'patience' value in table will not be editable, but will be updated with the calculation result.
Early Stopping
The Early Stopping callback can be set to stop training when a monitored quantity has stopped improving. For example if val_loss reaches a specific value, or if the results do not improve after a specific number of epochs. This can help prevent overfitting. A good idea when using early stopping is to choose a patience level that is coherent with the selected number of epochs. Refer to Early Stopping for information about setting the early stopping parameters.
Data Augmentation
The following Data Augmentation settings, which let you set compensate small training sets by simulating more data, are available on the Data Augmentation tab.
Data Augmentation tab
The performance of deep models often improve with the amount of data available, particularly the ability of models to generalize what they have learned to new images. A common way to compensate small training sets is to use data augmentation. If selected, different transformations will be applied to simulate more data than is actually available. Images may be flipped vertically or horizontally, rotated, sheared, or scaled. As such, specific data augmentation options should be chosen within the context of the training dataset. Refer to Data Augmentation Settings for information about modifying the data augmentation settings.

documents.title: Videos About the Segmentation Wizard
documents.text:
Videos About the Segmentation Wizard
The following videos provide an introduction to working with the Segmentation Wizard.
Additional videos are available in Dragonfly Social (https://dragonfly.comet.tech/en/resources/user-tutorials). You can also browse our YouTube Playlists (https://www.youtube.com/@dragonfly_software/playlists) to find topics of interest.
How to Prepare Your Data
The video below demonstrates how to efficiently prepare your data for the use with the Segmentation Wizard. It will show you how to crop your data, as well as invert and calibrate it.
Segmentation Wizard - Part 1: How to Prepare Your Data (07:24)
Topics Covered in the Video
The following topics are discussed in the video. Links to Help topics with further information are also provided.
Cropping your data to remove background regions (see Cropping Datasets).
Inverting axes so that the required view is in the image plane (see Inverting Datasets).
Calibrating image data so that it is less sensitive to intensity shifts (see Intensity Scale Calibration).
How to Create a Ground Truth and Train a Deep Learning Model
The video below demonstrates how to label your training set to crate a groundtruth and to then train a deep learning model to fully segment data.
Segmentation Wizard - Part 2: How to Create a Ground Truth and Train a Deep Learning Model (11:36)
Topics Covered in the Video
The following topics are discussed in the video. Links to Help topics with further information are also provided.
Creating and labeling frames for training deep models (see Labeling Frames for Training).
Using the ROI Painter tools (see ROI Painter).
Adding a region for visual feedback (see Enabling Visual Feedback and Checkpoint Caches).
Generating models (see Generating New Models).
Training models, evaluating predictions, and publishing models (see Training Models).
Applying models to segment the full dataset (see Segment with AI).

documents.path: Artificial Intelligence/Segmentation Wizard/Working with Multi-Modality Models.htm
documents.title: Working with Multi-Modality Models
documents.text:
Working with Multi-Modality Models
In some cases, you may want to work with a multi-modality images when training models with the Segmentation Wizard. For example, when you are working with data from simultaneous image acquisition systems or if you plan to paint on a filtered image that will not be included in the training data.
You can start a multi-modality session by selecting some or all of the required input images on the Data Properties and Settings panel (see Starting Multi-Modality Sessions from Selected Datasets), or you can start a multi-modality session from the Artificial Intelligence menu bar item (see Starting Multi-Modality Sessions from the Artificial Intelligence Menu). In either case, you can configure the inputs for the training set(s) in the Data Selection dialog before opening the Segmentation Wizard.
You should note the following whenever you work with multi-modality images:
All images in each training set must be registered and have the same geometry and shape.
An Image modalities box will appear at the top of the Input tab on the Segmentation Wizard panel, as shown below.
You can reorder and rename your datasets in the Image modalities box prior to training. As shown below, simply drag an item up or down in the list to reorder the inputs.
Note You will need to update all current deep models if you reorder the input image modalities. This option will appear after the inputs are reordered, as shown below.
Selecting an image in the list will automatically change the modality displayed in the workspace views and update the data selected for defining a range in the ROI Tools panel and for painting with the adaptive brushes and other ROI Painter tools. Defined ranges for each dataset will also be retained whenever you navigate between the different input images.
Note You can also use the keyboard shortcuts Show Next Image Modality and Show Previous Image Modality to change the modality displayed.
You can exclude an image modality from model training, as shown below, by unchecking its associated checkbox. In this case, the modality will only be used for labeling voxels.
Note You can include an image modality from model training by checking its associated checkbox.
You can choose different feature trees for each input of a machine learning (classical) model in the Model Generator dialog, as shown in the following screen capture.
Reopened Segmentation Wizard sessions will open automatically on the last modality that was visible in the workspace.
Starting Multi-Modality Sessions from Selected Datasets
You can start a multi-modality session by selecting some or all of the required input images on the Data Properties and Settings panel prior to launching the Segmentation Wizard.
How to Start a Multi-Modality Session from Selected Datasets
Select at least two of the input images on the Data Properties and Settings panel that you plan to include in the session.
Note The selected input datasets must be registered and have the same geometry and shape.
Right-click and then choose Segmentation Wizard in the pop-up menu.
The Data Selection dialog appears, as shown below.
Do the following, as required:
Select alternative inputs for 'Image 1' or 'Image 2' in the drop-down menu(s), as shown below.
Note Input order is important for multi-modality training and must be consistent when applying a trained model to a full dataset.
Add an image modality by clicking the Add Image Modality button, as shown below.
Note You will then need to select an input for the additional modality.
Note Input order is important for multi-modality training and must be consistent when applying a trained model to a full dataset.
Do the following to add an additional training set, if required:
Click the Add Dataset button, as shown below.
An additional dataset is added to the Inputs box.
Select the required inputs in the 'Image' drop-down menus for the new dataset, as shown below.
Note Input order is important for multi-modality training and must be consistent when applying a trained model to a full dataset.
Click the Continue button.
The Segmentation Wizard appears onscreen and the selected inputs appear on the Input tab in the Image modalities box, as shown below.
Note The Model Selection dialog will be shown before the Segmentation Wizard appears if a model that meets the input selection is already available.
Starting Multi-Modality Sessions from the Artificial Intelligence Menu
You can start a multi-modality session from the Artificial Intelligence menu bar item and then add the required image modalities in the Data Selection dialog.
How to Start a Multi-Modality Session from the Artificial Intelligence Menu
Choose Artificial Intelligence > Segmentation Wizard > New on the menu bar.
Click the Add Image Modality button, as shown below, to add an additional image modality to the current training set.
Select inputs for 'Image 1' or 'Image 2' in the drop-down menu(s), as shown below.
Add an image modality by clicking the Add Image Modality button, as shown below, and if required.
Note You will then need to select an input for the additional modality.
Note Input order is important for multi-modality training and must be consistent when applying a trained model to a full dataset.
Do the following to add an additional training set, if required:
Click the Add Dataset button, as shown below.
An additional dataset is added to the Inputs box.
Select the required inputs in the 'Image' drop-down menus for the new dataset, as shown below.
Note Input order is important for multi-modality training and must be consistent when applying a trained model to a full dataset.
Click the Continue button.
The Segmentation Wizard appears onscreen and the selected inputs appear on the Input tab in the Image modalities box, as shown below.
Note The Model Selection dialog will be shown before the Segmentation Wizard appears if a model that meets the input selection is already available.

documents.path: Artificial Intelligence/Segmentation Wizard/Working with Multiple Datasets.htm
documents.title: Working with Multiple Datasets
documents.text:
Working with Multiple Datasets
In some cases, you may want to work with a multiple images when training models with the Segmentation Wizard. For example, it may not always be possible to label an adequate number of pixels for training and validation on a single image. In this case, you can load multiple datasets to train your model.
You can start a multiple images session from the Artificial Intelligence menu bar item (see Starting Multiple Image Sessions from the Artificial Intelligence Menu) or you can start multiple image sessions by selecting some or all of the required input images on the Data Properties and Settings panel (see Starting Multiple Image Sessions from Selected Datasets). In either case, you can configure the inputs in the Data Selection dialog before opening the Segmentation Wizard.
You should note the following whenever you work with multiple image sessions:
A Data sets box will appear at the top of the Input tab on the Segmentation Wizard panel, as shown below.
Each dataset in the list will have its own set of frames.
Selecting a dataset in the list will automatically change the image displayed in the workspace views and update the data selected for defining a range in the ROI Tools panel and for painting with the adaptive brushes and other ROI Painter tools. Defined ranges for each data set will also be retained whenever you navigate between the different images.
Reopened Segmentation Wizard sessions will open automatically on the last dataset that was visible in the workspace.
Starting Multiple Image Sessions from the Artificial Intelligence Menu
You can start a multiple image session from the Artificial Intelligence menu bar item and then add the required datasets in the Data Selection dialog.
How to Start a Multiple Image Session from the Artificial Intelligence Menu
Choose Artificial Intelligence > Segmentation Wizard > New on the menu bar.
The Data Selection dialog appears.
Select an input in the 'Image' drop-down menu, as shown below.
Click the Add Dataset button, as shown below.
An additional dataset is added to the Inputs box.
Select the required input(s) in the 'Image' drop-down menu(s) for the new dataset, as shown below.
Add additional training sets, as required, and select the required input(s) in the 'Image' drop-down menu(s).
Click the Continue button.
The Segmentation Wizard appears onscreen and the selected inputs appear on the Input tab in the Data sets box, as shown below.
Note The Model Selection dialog will be shown before the Segmentation Wizard appears if a model that meets the input selection is already available.
Starting Multiple Image Sessions from Selected Datasets
You can start a multiple image session by selecting some or all of the required input images on the Data Properties and Settings panel prior to launching the Segmentation Wizard.
How to Start a Multiple Image Session from Selected Datasets
Select at least two of the input images on the Data Properties and Settings panel that you plan to include in the session.
Right-click and then choose Segmentation Wizard in the pop-up menu.
The Data Selection dialog appears, as shown below.
Note The default setting for starting sessions with multiple datasets is for multi-modality training. You will need to reduce the number of input images for each dataset, unless you are training with multi-modality images.
Click the Remove Image Modality button, as shown below, if your training session will use single images instead of multi-modality images.
Click the Add Dataset button, as shown below.
An additional dataset is added to the Inputs box.
Select the required input(s) in the 'Image' drop-down menu(s) for the new dataset, as shown below.
Add additional training sets, as required, and select the required input(s) in the 'Image' drop-down menu(s).
Click the Continue button.
The Segmentation Wizard appears onscreen and the selected inputs appear on the Input tab in the Data sets box, as shown below.
Note The Model Selection dialog will be shown before the Segmentation Wizard appears if a model that meets the input selection is already available.

documents.path: Dragonfly Organizer/Accessing and Adding Remote Servers.htm
documents.title: Accessing and Adding Remote Servers
documents.text:
Accessing and Adding Remote Servers
You can search for and open projects saved on remote servers that have enabled sharing and that are connected within your network.
Accessing Network Hosted Data (on Windows)
Because the Organizer runs under the umbrella of Windows services, you may encounter certain limitations accessing network hosted data on Windows.
Windows services run under designated users, who usually don't have access to network drive mappings. This is strictly configuration related, meaning that you may run into some issues depending on how your IT department configured the network. For example, sometimes UNC (universal naming convention) notated paths won't work, other times they will. The Dragonfly support team has not been able to determine exactly what configuration parameters affect this or not, but two alternate methods of accessing network data are recommended. For example, when you want to add a root on a network.
Method 1… Use normal UNC paths. A UNC path uses double slashes or backslashes to precede the name of the computer. The path (disk and directories) within the computer are separated with a single slash or backslash, as in the following example. Note that in the example below, drive letters (c:, d:, and so on) are not used.
\\servername\some_path
Method 2… If you see network errors in the Organizer logs, the workaround is to use the IP address of the network resource. In this case, the IP address of that network resource must be fixed, which is normally the case.
Instead of designating the root with UNC, for example:
\\servername\some_path
You'll need to define the root like this instead:
\\192.168.0.xx\some_path (in which 192.168.0.xx is the correct IP address).
Adding Remote Servers
The following is required to access and search for projects saved on remote servers within your network:
Sharing for the Organizer must be enabled on the remote server.
The IP address of the server that you want to access (see Accessing Network Hosted Data (on Windows)).
The password of the remote server's Organizer, if authentication is enabled.
In addition, you must make sure that you can communicate with the remote server. In some cases, communication may be restricted by a firewall. In such cases, the port used by the remote system's Organizer must be opened. Refer to the documentation related to the firewall's security settings for more information.
How to Add a Remote Server
Click the Sources tab on the Organizer dialog.
Click the Add button.
The Remote Server dialog appears.
Do the following:
Enter the IP address of the remote server that you want to access.
Enter the port number used by the remote server to communicate with Dragonfly's Organizer.
Enter a description for the remote server.
Click the Verify button to test the connection, recommended.
Click OK.
The remote server is added to the Sources list.
Note Remote servers may require authentication, in which case you will need the password when you search such servers.
Add additional remote servers, if required.
Modifying Remote Servers
If required, you can modify the settings of a configured remote server.
How to Modify a Remote Server
Click the Sources tab on the Organizer dialog.
Select the remote server that you need to modify.
Click the Modify button.
The Remote Server dialog appears.
Do the following, as required:
Edit the IP address of the remote server.
Edit the port number used by the remote server to communicate with Dragonfly's Organizer.
Edit the description of the remote server.
Click the Verify button to retest the connection, recommended.
Click OK to apply your updates.
Removing Remote Servers
If required, you can remove a configured remote server from the Sources panel.
How to Remove a Remote Server
Click the Sources tab on the Organizer dialog.
Select the remote server that you want to remove.
Click the Remove button.
Click OK.

documents.path: Dragonfly Organizer/Adding and Editing Root Folders.htm
documents.title: Adding and Editing Root Folders
documents.text:
Adding and Editing Root Folders
Options to add, edit, and remove root folders are available in Organizer Settings dialog on the Roots panel, shown below.
Organizer Settings dialog
Name… Is the assigned name of the root folder.
Folder… Indicates the location of the root folder.
Share… Indicates if the folder is shared (checked) or not shared (unchecked). See Enabling Sharing for information about enabling sharing.
Projects Count… Indicates the number of projects in the folder.
Adding Root Folders
You will need to add at least one root folder to the Organizer before you can create a project. You can also add multiple root folders to further organize your data, as well as to allow sharing of specific folders.
How to Add a Root Folder
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar of the Organizer dialog.
The Organizer Settings dialog appears.
Click Roots in the Navigation pane.
The Roots panel appears in the dialog.
Click the Add a Root button.
The Root dialog appears.
Do the following, as required:
Enter a name for the new root folder.
Enter a folder path or click Browse and then select a folder in the Choose a Project Root Folder dialog. If required, you can create a new folder.
Check the Share option, if you want to share the contents of the folder with other users (see Enabling Sharing).
Click Apply or OK to save your changes.
The new root appears in the Roots panel.
Editing Root Folders
A number of options are available for editing root folders. You can rename root folders, change folders, and enable or disable sharing.
How to Edit a Root Folder
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar of the Organizer dialog.
The Organizer Settings dialog appears.
Click Roots in the Navigation pane.
The Roots panel appears in the dialog.
Select the root folder that you want to edit.
Click Edit Root.
The Root dialog appears.
Do the following, as required:
Enter a new name for the root folder.
Edit the folder path or click Browse and then select a folder in the Choose a Project Root Folder dialog. If required, you can create a new folder.
Check or uncheck the Share option (see Enabling Sharing).
Click Apply or OK to save your changes.
Removing Root Folders
If required, you can remove a root folder from the Organizer.
Whenever you remove a root folder, all data contained in the project folders will be retained. You need to delete a project to remove data (see Deleting Projects).
How to Remove a Root Folder
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar of the Organizer dialog.
The Organizer Settings dialog appears.
Click Roots in the Navigation pane.
The Roots panel appears in the dialog.
Select the root folder that you want to remove.
Note Whenever you remove a root folder, all data contained in the project folders will be retained.
Click Remove Root.
Click Apply or OK to save your changes.

documents.title: Adding Data to Projects
documents.text:
Adding Data to Projects
You can add data, such as items in the Data Properties and Settings panel, trained deep models and machine learning classifiers, as well as screenshots, CSV files, PDFs, and videos to a project. In addition, you can add tags to each item in a project to facilitate searching.
How to Add Data to a Project
Do one of the following:
Create a new project (see Creating New Projects).
Open a project (see Searching for Projects).
Expand the project and then do the following, as required:
Drag-and-drop a selected item or items from the Data Properties and Settings panel to the project.
Note You can load these items by dragging them to the workspace or to the Data Properties and Settings panel (see Loading Data from Projects).
Drag-and-drop trained models from the model list in the Deep Learning Tool or trained classifiers from the Machine Learning Segmentation dialog.
Note You can load a model from a project by dragging it to the Model list in the Deep Learning Tool or Machine Learning Segmentation dialog.
Drag-and-drop the Camera icon from a view to save a screenshot of the view. You can enter a description for the screenshot in the Screenshot dialog before it is added to the project.
Drag-and-drop items, such as CSV files, PDFs, and videos, from your file browser to the saved data list.
Click Save current session to project to save the current session to the project.
Add tags to each data item, recommended.
To add an Item tag, selected the required item in the project and then add the tag(s) in the Item tags box on the left sidebar, as shown below.
Note Each tag you add must be on a separate line.
How to Delete Data From a Project
Expand the required project.
Select the item that you want to delete and then click the Delete Item button, as shown below.
Click Yes to confirm the action or No to cancel.

documents.path: Dragonfly Organizer/Adding Project and Item Tags.htm
documents.title: Adding Project and Item Tags
documents.text:
Adding Project and Item Tags
To facilitate searching, you can add tags to projects and to items in a project. Project and Item tags appear in the Tags box on the left sidebar for the selected project or item, as shown below.
Project tags
See Setting Up Project Tags for information about setting up mandatory and optional project tags.
How to Add Project Tags
Select the required project in the Project list.
Click inside the Project tags box and then enter a new tag.
Add additional tags, as required.
Note Each tag must appear on a new line. Press Enter to create a new line.
How to Add Item Tags
Select the required item in a project.
Click inside the Item tags box and then enter a new tag.
Add additional tags, as required.
Note Each tag must appear on a new line. Press Enter to create a new line.

documents.title: Configuring the Network Settings
documents.text:
Configuring the Network Settings
The Network settings, shown below, display the IP address of your system and let you choose a server port. You should note that you will need to provide this information to anyone you plan to share projects with.
Organizer Settings dialog
How to Configure the Network Settings
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar of the Organizer dialog.
The Organizer Settings dialog appears.
Click Network in the Navigation pane.
The Network panel appears in the dialog.
Enter a port number in the Server port edit box.
Note The default server port, 80, should be sufficient for most installations.
Click Apply or OK to save your changes.

documents.title: Creating and Editing Projects
documents.text:
Creating and Editing Projects
You can create a new project in the Organizer whenever you need to save work on a particular dataset or topic. Click the New Project button on the left sidebar to open the Create a Project dialog, shown below.
Create a Project dialog
Creating New Projects
You will need to add at least one root folder before you can create a new project (see Adding and Editing Root Folders). You should also select all other required Organizer settings, such as sharing and project tags, before you create your first project (see Organizer Settings).
How to Create a New Project
Choose File > Open the Organizer on the menu bar.
The Organizer dialog appears.
If required, you can add a new root folder before you create a new project (see Adding and Editing Root Folders).
Click the New Project button on the left sidebar.
The Create a Project dialog appears.
Do the following in the Create a Project dialog:
Enter a name for your new project.
Select a root folder in the Root drop-down menu.
Enter any mandatory tags that are required, as well as any optional tags (see Setting Up Project Tags for information about adding mandatory and optional project tags).
Add other tags to help searching for the project, optional.
Click OK to create the project.
The project appears in the Project list (see Adding Data to Projects for information about adding data to your new project).
Renaming Projects
If required, you can rename projects.
How to Rename a Project
Search for the project that you want to rename, if required (see Searching for Projects).
Select the project that you want to rename in the Project list.
Click the … button and then choose Rename Project in the drop-down menu, as shown below.
Enter a new name in the Rename Project dialog.
Click OK to rename the current project.
Deleting Projects
If required, you can delete projects. In this case, all files within the project will also be deleted.
How to Delete a Project
Select the project that you want in the Project list.
Click the Delete Project button.
Click Yes if you want to delete the project and all related files.

documents.title: Customizing the Interface
documents.text:
Customizing the Interface
The Interface settings, shown below, let you choose how items appear in listed projects. You can specify a width and height for items, as well as choose a font size.
Organizer Settings dialog
How to Customize the Interface
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar of the Organizer dialog.
The Organizer Settings dialog appears.
Click Interface in the Navigation pane.
The Interface panel appears in the dialog.
Do the following, as required.
Set the maximum width, in pixels, for project items.
Set the height, in pixels, for project items.
Choose a font size for project items.
Click Apply or OK to save your changes.

documents.title: Dragonfly Organizer
documents.text:
Dragonfly Organizer
Dragonfly's Organizer, which is enterprise ready for centralizing data within an institute, is equipped with drag-and-drop functionality so that you can readily add objects — such as image data, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, screen captures, session files, and more — to a project from the current session and vice versa. You can create root folders and sub-roots that can hold multiple project folders, add tags to a project for easy searching, 'Star' and 'Pin' frequently referenced projects, as well as move, rename, merge, and delete projects. You can search local drives and remote servers for matching tags, data types, or by date, as well as protect your private data while sharing your public projects with other users.
In This Section
Organizer Dialog
Organizer Settings
Creating and Editing Projects
Adding Data to Projects
Adding Project and Item Tags
Loading Data from Projects
Searching for Projects
Accessing and Adding Remote Servers

documents.title: Enabling Sharing
documents.text:
Enabling Sharing
The Sharing settings, shown below, let you enable sharing and to require authentication for remote access.
Organizer Settings dialog
You can specify which folders will be shared whenever you add or edit your root folders (see Adding and Editing Root Folders).
How to Enable Sharing
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar of the Organizer dialog.
The Organizer Settings dialog appears.
Click Sharing in the Navigation pane.
The Sharing panel appears in the dialog.
Check the Enable sharing option, if you want to share your projects with other users.
Note See Adding and Editing Root Folders for information about adding shared roots.
Check the Authenticate access option and then enter a password in the Password edit box, if you can require authentication for remote access.
Note The selected password should respect the cybersecurity guidelines set by your institution or facility.
Note You will need to supply the selected password, as well as your IP address and configured server port, to any users authorized to access your shared projects. See Configuring the Network Settings for information about IP addresses and server ports.
Click Apply or OK to save your changes.

documents.title: Loading Data from Projects
documents.text:
Loading Data from Projects
How you load data from a project depends on the type of fie you need to access — Dragonfly Object files, Session files, deep models, machine learning classifiers, or other types of files.
Loading Images and other Object Files
Do any of the following to load items that were saved in the Dragonfly Object file format, such as images, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, meshes, and session groups:
Drag an item or items from the Organizer to the Dragonfly workspace or to the Data Properties and Settings panel, as shown below.
Double-click an item to add it to the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Loading Session Files
Do the following to load a session file that was saved in the Organizer:
Drag the session file from the Organizer to the Dragonfly workspace.
Note In this case, the current session will be cleared.
Loading Deep Models
Any deep model that was saved to the Organizer can be loaded into Dragonfly's Deep Learning Tool for further training or inference.
Do the following to load a deep model from a project:
Open the Deep Learning Tool.
Drag the required model from the Organizer to the Model list on the Model Overview panel.
Loading Machine Learning Classifiers
Any Machine Learning classifier that was saved to the Organizer can be loaded into Dragonfly's Machine Learning Segmentation dialog for further training or inference.
Do the following to load a Machine Learning classifier from a project:
Open the Machine Learning Segmentation dialog.
Drag the required classifier from the Organizer to the Model list on the Model panel.
Opening Other Types of Files
Do the following to open other types of files, such as PDFs, CSVs, screen captures, and videos, from a project:
Double-click an item to open it in an associated program.

documents.title: Organizer Dialog
documents.text:
Organizer Dialog
The Organizer dialog includes a Search panel that incorporates a number of options for locating projects and data, a Project list panel that lists found and pinned projects, as well as a left sidebar that lists Starred and Recent projects, project tags, and lets you access the Settings dialog.
Choose File > Open the Organizer on the menu bar to open the Organizer dialog, as shown below.
Organizer dialog
A. Left sidebar B. Search panel C. Project list panel D. Status bar
Left Sidebar
The Organizer dialog includes a left sidebar that lists Starred and Recent projects, project and item tags, and lets you access the Settings dialog and create a new project.
Starred… All 'Starred' projects appear in this easy-to-access list.
Recent… Recently accessed projects are listed here. If required, you clear the list by right-clicking and then choosing Clear Recent List. The maximum number of projects that appear in the list can be set as a preference (see Organizer Preferences).
Tags… Displays the tags that were added to the currently selected project (Project tags) or to the selected object (Item tags). See Setting Up Project Tags and Adding Project and Item Tags
Settings… Opens the Organizer Settings dialog, in which you can customize the size of project items, choose a database location, setup mandatory and optional project tags, enable sharing, and rebuild the database (see Organizer Settings).
New Project… Opens the Create a Project dialog, in which you can setup a new project (see Creating New Projects).
Search Panel
Multiple search criteria are available on the Search panel to help you locate projects and associated data on local and remote servers (see Searching for Projects).
Project List Panel
All pinned projects, as well as projects that match the current search criteria, appear in the Project list panel. You should note that each project can be expanded to view the available data or collapsed to maximize space in the dialog, as shown below.
Project List panel
The options available for listed projects are summarized below.
Options for listed projects
Icon
Description
Expand/Collapse
+/-
Lets you expand or collapse a listed project.
Starred
Lets you 'star' a project. Starred projects are listed in the 'Starred' box on the left sidebar.
Pinned
Lets you 'pin' a project. Pinned projects will appear at the top of the Project list panel at all times.
Project name (Project details)
NA
Indicates the name of a project. Additional information about a project, such as the root folder(s) and last modified date and time can also be shown by selecting Show project details on the bottom right of the Organizer dialog.
Project Options*
…
Lets you access additional options for a project.
Rename Project… Opens the Rename Project dialog, in which you can enter a new name for a project (see Renaming Projects).
Open Folder… Opens the folder that contains the current project in Window's File Browser or in the installed file browser for Linux.
Update*
Automatically updates objects that are loaded in the current scene.
Move*
Lets you move the current project to another root folder. You can choose a new root folder in the Select a Root dialog.
Delete*
Lets you delete the current project (see Deleting Projects).
* Theses items only appear when you hover over title bar a listed project.
Status Bar
Indicates the number of projects shown in the Project list and lets you show or hide the project details.

documents.title: Organizer Settings
documents.text:
Organizer Settings
You can configure the Organizer by customizing the size and look of project items, adding root folders, setting-up mandatory and optional project tags, and enabling sharing. Maintenance items, such as rebuilding the database, are also available in the Organizer Settings dialog.
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar to open the Organizer Settings dialog, shown below.
Organizer Settings dialog
Interface… Lets you customize the size and look of project items (see Customizing the Interface).
Network… Lets you view your current IP address and specify a server port (see Configuring the Network Settings).
Roots… Lets you add and edit root folders (see Adding and Editing Root Folders).
Project Tags… Lets you setup tags that are mandatory or optional when a new project is created (see Setting Up Project Tags).
Sharing… Lets you enable sharing (see Enabling Sharing).
Maintenance… Lets you rebuild the database (see Rebuilding the Database).

documents.title: Rebuilding the Database
documents.text:
Rebuilding the Database
Rebuilding the database may be required if the file is corrupted or if you deleted root or project folders outside of Dragonfly. You can rebuild the database file at any time.
Open the Organizer Settings dialog and then click Maintenance in the Navigation panel to access the option to rebuild the dataset.
Organizer Settings dialog
The following will occur when the database file, which is stored in: %programdata%\ORS\dataorganizer, is rebuilt:
The current database file is deleted.
A new database file is reconstructed by scanning all files in the root and project folders.
How to Rebuild the Database
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar of the Organizer dialog.
The Organizer Settings dialog appears.
Click Maintenance in the Navigation pane.
Click Rebuild Database.
Note Rebuilding the local database can be a lengthy process, particularly if a large number of files are available.

documents.title: Searching for Projects
documents.text:
Searching for Projects
The Organizer dialog provides a number of search options to help you quickly find saved projects on local and remote servers. Projects that match the selected search criteria are added to the Projects list.
Main search tab
Main search… The Main search tab provides a number of options to search for matching projects. You can search projects for matching tags and text, such as the name of the items in projects, or you can search for types of objects. In addition, you can apply other criteria in the Dates, Sources, and Local roots tabs.
Click the Search button to find projects that match the selected search criteria. You should note that if no search criteria is entered in the Find box and all types of objects are selected, the results will be all saved projects on the selected sources and local roots.
Dates… Items on the Dates tab let you limit searches to projects created before, after, or between specific dates or that were last modified before, after, or between specific dates.
Sources… You can select the local and remote servers to search on the Sources tab.
Local roots… Lets extend or limit your search to specific local root folders.
How to Search for a Project
Do the following, as required:
Click the Dates tab if you want to limit your search to projects created before, after, or between specific dates or that were last modified before, after, or between specific dates. These options are available in the Create date and Last modified date boxes, as shown below.
Check all of the sources that you want to search on the Sources tab, shown below.
Note Refer to the topic Accessing and Adding Remote Servers for information about connecting to network servers.
Check all of the local root folders that you want to search on the Local roots tab, as shown below.
Note Refer to the topic Adding and Editing Root Folders for information about adding and editing root folders.
Select the search criteria as follows:
Enter the text that you are searching for in the Find box.
In this case, the Organizer will search for matching projects and matching items in projects, as well as matching project and item tags.
Select the types of objects that you are searching for by choosing one of more of the Find objects of types items. In this case, the Organizer will search for objects that match the selected type(s).
Click the Search button.
All projects that match the search criteria are listed in the Projects list.
Expand a matching project to view the available items.
Note Refer to the topic Loading Data from Projects for information about loading different data types.

documents.title: Setting Up Project Tags
documents.text:
Setting Up Project Tags
In some cases, you may want to make specific project tags a mandatory or optional requirement for creating a new project. Whenever you add this requirement, the mandatory and optional tags will appear in the Create a Project dialog as shown below whenever you create a new project. You should note that project tags can also be added after you create a new project (see Adding Project and Item Tags).
Create a Project dialog
How to Add Project Tags
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar of the Organizer dialog.
The Organizer Settings dialog appears.
Click Project Tags in the Navigation pane.
The Project Tags panel appears in the dialog.
Click Add in the Project Tags panel.
A new tag is added.
Do the following, as required:
Double-click inside the caption box and then enter a name for the project tag, as shown below.
Check the Mandatory box if you want to make entering the tag mandatory whenever you create a new project.
Uncheck the Mandatory box if you want to make entering the tag optional whenever you create a new project.
Add additional project tags, as required.
Click Apply or OK to save your changes.
How to Remove Project Tags
Click the Settings button on the left sidebar of the Organizer dialog.
The Organizer Settings dialog appears.
Click Project Tags in the Navigation pane.
The Project Tags panel appears in the dialog.
Select the project tag that you want to remove.
Click Remove in the Project Tags panel.
Remove additional project tags, as required.
Click Apply or OK to save your changes.

documents.path: Exporting and Saving Data/Copying Screenshots to the Clipboard.htm
documents.title: Copying Screenshots to the Clipboard
documents.text:
Copying Screenshots to the Clipboard
Screenshots of the current view, which can include its scale bar, legend, annotations, overlays, and other objects that are visible onscreen, can be copied to your clipboard and then pasted into another application, such as Microsoft Word or Paint.
How to Copy a Screenshot to the Clipboard
Select the required view and then adjust your image accordingly. You can adjust the zoom, pan, and window levels, as well as add annotations to highlight particular areas of interest.
Click the Camera icon on the top right of the view.
A screenshot of the selected view is copied to the clipboard.
Paste the contents of the clipboard into another application.

documents.path: Exporting and Saving Data/Exporting and Saving Data.htm
documents.title: Exporting and Saving Data
documents.text:
Exporting and Saving Data
A number of different options are available in Dragonfly if you need to save or export processed image data or generated objects, such as regions of interest and multi-ROIs. You can also save the current state of the workspace, including all imported, processed, or created objects, in a session file .
In This Section
Managing User Data
Exporting Objects
Exporting Images
Exporting Images as RGB
Exporting Images in the DICOM Format
Exporting Screenshots
Copying Screenshots to the Clipboard

documents.path: Exporting and Saving Data/Exporting Images as RGB.htm
documents.title: Exporting Images as RGB
documents.text:
Exporting Images as RGB
You can export selected RGB channels in the BMP, JPEG, and PNG file formats to retain color in exported images.
Select the required red-green-blue channels, right-click, and then choose Export > As RGB in the pop-up menu to open the Export as RGB dialog, shown below.
Export as RGB dialog
You can drag channels up and down to match them to a specific output in the Export as RGB dialog, as well as replace channels as required.
How to Export Images as RGB
Select the required red-green-blue channels in the Data Properties and Settings panel, right-click, and then choose Export > As RGB in the pop-up menu.
The Export as RGB dialog appears.
Do the following if you need to reorder the selected channels:
Drag the channel that you need to move to a new location, as shown below.
Do the following if you need to replace a channel with another one:
Select the channel that you need to remove.
Click the Remove button.
Drag the replacement channel into the dialog from the Data Properties and Settings panel, as shown below.
Click the Export button.
Select a destination folder and file name, as well as a file format, in the Save As dialog.
Click the Save button.

documents.path: Exporting and Saving Data/Exporting Images in the DICOM Format.htm
documents.title: Exporting Images in the DICOM Format
documents.text:
Exporting Images in the DICOM Format
You can export image data from the Data Properties and Settings panel in the DICOM format.
Right-click the data you want to export in the Data Properties and Settings panel and then choose Export > As DICOM in the pop-up menu to open the Export as DICOM Images dialog, shown below.
Export as DICOM Images dialog
DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine) is a standard for handling, storing, printing, and transmitting information in medical imaging. It includes a file format definition and a network communications protocol that uses TCP/IP to communicate between systems. DICOM files (*.dcm extension) can be exchanged between two entities that are capable of receiving images and data in DICOM format.
How to Export Images in the DICOM Format
Right-click the data you want to export in the Data Properties and Settings panel and then choose Export > As DICOM in the pop-up menu.
The Export as DICOM Images dialog appears.
Select a destination folder, as follows:
Enter the path to the destination folder.
Click the Browse button and then choose a folder in the Select Output Folder dialog.
Click OK to export the selected images.
Click OK in the Export to DICOM message box.

documents.title: Exporting Images
documents.text:
Exporting Images
You can export image data from the Data Properties and Settings panel to a number of standard file formats, including RAW, TIFF, JPEG, MRC, and other standard and proprietary formats.
Right-click the image data that you want to export in the Data Properties and Settings panel and then choose Export > Image in the pop-up menu to open the Save As dialog, as shown below.
Save As dialog
The following formats and options are available in the Save As dialog for exporting images.
The Save As options are not available for Linux versions of Dragonfly.
Apply W/L and gamma… If selected, the window leveling settings and gamma value you selected for reviewing images will be applied to exported image data. You should note that this option is only available for Dragonfly 3D World ZEISS edition. Contact Comet Technologies Canada Inc. for information about the availability of this version of Dragonfly.
Export formats
Description
RAW (*.raw)
Saves images as raw pixel data without a header. Suitable for transferring files between applications and computer platforms.
Note When saving RAW files in Dragonfly, header information is saved in an accompanying DAT file.
TIFF (*.tif; *.tiff)
One of the most widely supported lossless compression file formats for storing bit-mapped images, Tagged Image File Format (TIFF) files can be uncompressed or compressed.
The additional options for saving images in the TIFF file format include the following:
Use LZW compression… If selected, LZW compression will be applied to exported TIFFs. You should note that LZW, invented by Abraham Lempel, Jacob Ziv, and Terry Welch, is a lossless compression method. That means that no data will be lost in compression, unlike a lossy format like JPG. You can open and save a TIFF file as many times you like without degrading the image.
Output all images into one file… If selected, all distinct images within the image stack will be saved within one multi-image TIFF file.
Note Image spacing values in the X and Y axes are retained when exporting to the TIFF file format, but are not retained when exporting to BMP, JPEG, or PNG.
JPEG2000 (*.jp2)
The lossy JPEG2000 file format can provide better compression performance with improved image quality compared to the original JPEG file format. A higher dynamic range is also supported by this format, with no limit to image bit depth.
Analyze 7.5 (*.hdr)
The Analyze file format was developed at the Mayo Clinic as part of a software package of the same name. Datasets in this format consist of small HDR files that describe the data and IMG files with the raw data.
MRC (*.mrc)
A file format for electron density that has become an industry standard in cryo-electron microscopy. It was developed by the MRC (Medical Research Council) Laboratory of Molecular Biology.
Note Available for unsigned short (16 bits) and float (32 bits) data types only.
JPEG (*.jpg)
A standard format that stores images in a compressed form. JPG lossy compression can lead to artifacts that may not be compatible with quantitative analyzes.
JPEG image quality… The JPG format is lossy compressed according to a quality value, which can range from 100 — the highest quality, but also the largest file size — down to 1, which creates a poor quality, small file.
Note Available for 8 bit images only.
BMP (*.bmp)
Standard uncompressed bit-mapped graphics format used primarily in Windows.
Note Available for 8 bit images only.
PNG (*.png)
The Portable Network Graphics (PNG) format is a more powerful alternative to the GIF file format. PNGs are stored in compressed form using a lossless compression algorithm. The format is also able to store an alpha channel.
Note Available for 8 bit images only.
Dragonfly (*.ORSObject)
These files are proprietary binary formatted files for Dragonfly in which data is written sequentially and XML (Extensible Markup Language) is appended after the binary data.
How to Export Images
Apply the required window leveling and/or gamma settings to the images you plan to export, if required (see Window Leveling).
Right-click the required dataset in the Data Properties and Settings panel and then choose Export > Images in the pop-up menu.
Select a destination folder and file name, as well as a file format, in the Save As dialog.
Select the required options for the chosen file format, as required.
Click the Save button.

documents.title: Exporting Objects
documents.text:
Exporting Objects
You can export loaded objects, such as images, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, and annotations, in the Dragonfly Object (*.ORSObject extension) file format. Dragonfly Object files are proprietary binary formatted files in which data is written
sequentially and XML (Extensible Markup Language) is appended after the
binary data. Multiple objects can be exported to a single Dragonfly Object file or you can choose to export multiple objects as separate files to a folder.
You can also export image data to a number of different file formats, including RAW, TIFF, BMP, and others (see Exporting Images).
How To Export as a Dragonfly Object File
Do one of the following:
Right-click the required object(s) in the Data Properties and Settings panel and then choose Export > As ORSObject in the pop-up menu.
Select the required object(s) in the Data Properties and Settings panel and then click the Export icon at the bottom of the list.
The Export to File dialog appears.
Select a destination folder and file name in the Save As dialog.
Click the Save button.
How to Export as Multiple Dragonfly Object Files
Select the objects you need to export in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Right-click and then choose Export > As Multiple ORSObject in the pop-up menu.
Select a target folder in the Select Output Directory dialog and then click the Select Folder button.
The files are exported to the selected folder. The name assigned to each object, as it appears in the Data Properties and Settings panel, is used to identify the different exported files.
Note If the selected items share the same name, their file names will be appended with a sequential number.
Click the Save button.

documents.title: Exporting Screenshots
documents.text:
Exporting Screenshots
A number of options are available in Dragonfly to export screenshots of the active view — including its scale bar, legend, annotations, overlays, and other objects that are visible onscreen — to a number of standard image file formats. The additional option to accumulate and then export multiple screenshots is available on the Multiple Screenshots panel.
Screenshots of the current view can also be copied to your clipboard and then pasted into another application, such as Microsoft Word or Paint (see Copying Screenshots to the Clipboard). In addition, you can capture fullscreen screenshots of Dragonfly (see Capturing Fullscreen Screenshots).
Exporting Screenshots From the Scene's Views Properties Panel and From Views
The Export Screenshot option, which is available on the Scene's Views Properties panel and from the views pop-menu, allows you to scale an image to a specified width or height to create files that are suitable for presentations, publications, and large displays. You can also choose to export screenshots without a background from 3D views.
How to Export a Screenshot From the Scene's Views Properties Panel or From a View
Select the required view and then adjust your image accordingly. You can adjust the zoom, pan, and window levels, as well as add annotations to highlight particular areas of interest.
Do one of the following:
Click the Export Screenshot button in the Scene Views Properties panel.
Right-click inside a view and then choose Export Screenshot of View in the pop-up menu.
The Screenshot Size dialog appears.
Do the following in the Screenshot Size dialog:
Enter the required width or height in the appropriate dimension box.
The dimensions will be constrained to match the aspect ratio of the view. Changing the width will automatically affect the height of the image and vice-versus.
The maximum dimension may be limited. This limitation is based on the capability of your system and the type of view selected — 2D or 3D. You should also note that the maximum dimension possible for 3D views is 4096 pixels.

documents.title: Exporting Images as RGB

Exporting Images as RGB
You can export selected RGB channels in the BMP, JPEG, and PNG file formats to retain color in exported images.

How to Export Images as RGB
Select the required red-green-blue channels in the Data Properties and Settings panel, right-click, and then choose Export > As RGB in the pop-up menu.
The Export as RGB dialog appears.
Do the following if you need to reorder the selected channels:
Drag the channel that you need to move to a new location, as shown below.
Do the following if you need to replace a channel with another one:
Select the channel that you need to remove.
Click the Remove button.
Drag the replacement channel into the dialog from the Data Properties and Settings panel, as shown below.
Click the Export button.
Select a destination folder and file name, as well as a file format, in the Save As dialog.
Click the Save button.
